impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a trial court must defer to the terms of an existing license agreement to assess copyright infringement damages, and what constitutes permissible use of the 'book of wisdom' in calculating such damages against the government.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that courts need not defer to license agreement terms when assessing copyright infringement damages, approving instead a hypothetical negotiation approach. However, the court vacated the $12.68 million damages award in part, finding the trial court adopted a legally impermissible view of the 'book of wisdom' doctrine and assessed non-compensatory damages. This case addresses how courts value unauthorized government use of copyrighted software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software companies and copyright holders benefit from the court's endorsement of flexible damages methodologies not tethered to existing license rates, potentially allowing higher recovery in infringement cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: The ruling constrains damages models by prohibiting non-compensatory damages and limiting how post-infringement evidence (book of wisdom) can inflate damage awards, potentially reducing recoveries in some cases.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the plaintiff presented legally sufficient evidence that each of its four asserted trade secrets was a protectable trade secret under California law, and whether ideas that are generally known can constitute an inventive contribution for patent inventorship purposes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable under California law. The court also reversed on patent invalidity, holding that generally known ideas cannot constitute inventive contributions. The counterfeiting claim and damages were affirmed. This significantly raises the evidentiary bar for trade secret plaintiffs in the medical device industry.
impacts.positiveImplications: Businesses accused of trade secret misappropriation benefit from the court's rigorous application of the requirement to prove each trade secret is protectable, providing a stronger defense framework.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret holders face heightened evidentiary burdens to establish that asserted trade secrets are protectable, potentially undermining enforcement efforts, particularly where the information overlaps with generally known concepts.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding a trade secret damages expert's testimony and whether it properly assessed damages for trade secret misappropriation and breach of contract related to automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to consider two previously rejected damages models. The court reversed the breach of contract damages ruling and reinstated the jury award, while affirming liability for trade secret misappropriation. This case has major implications for how damages are calculated in complex software trade secret cases involving technology licensing relationships.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors benefit from the court's broader acceptance of damages methodologies and the reinstatement of jury-awarded contract damages, strengthening remedies for misappropriation by licensees.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology licensees face increased exposure as courts are directed to consider a wider range of damages models in trade secret cases arising from terminated licensing relationships.

impacts.caseName: Insulet Corp. v. EOFlow, Co. Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the statute of limitations under the Defend Trade Secrets Act had expired before Insulet brought suit against EOFlow for misappropriation of insulin patch pump trade secrets.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the jury verdict and district court judgment in favor of Insulet, holding that as a matter of law the DTSA's statute of limitations had expired before suit was filed. The court found that Insulet knew or should have known of the alleged misappropriation more than three years before filing. This decision provides critical guidance on when the DTSA limitations period begins to run in cases involving former employees sharing confidential information with competitors.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of trade secret misappropriation gain a stronger statute of limitations defense, particularly where the trade secret owner had early indicators of potential misappropriation but delayed suit.
impacts.negativeImplications: Trade secret owners must act promptly upon learning of potential misappropriation or risk losing their DTSA claims entirely, creating pressure to file suit based on incomplete information.

impacts.caseName: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. ecobee Technologies ULC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in using a single verdict form question covering infringement for all asserted patents and in its handling of patent eligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101 for wireless building automation system patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the $11.5 million infringement and damages judgments, finding the single-question verdict form covering all asserted patents was reversible error, and remanded for a new trial on infringement and damages. The court also vacated the § 101 determination for one patent under Alice step two while affirming eligibility for others. This decision reinforces the requirement for patent-specific jury findings in multi-patent cases.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in multi-patent infringement cases benefit from the requirement for patent-specific verdict forms, preventing plaintiffs from obtaining sweeping judgments without proving infringement of each patent.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting multiple patents face greater procedural complexity and risk, as a single flawed verdict form can unravel an entire damages award across all asserted patents.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communications are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents relating to non-uniform constellation designs used in digital communications, while affirming eligibility for the '509 and '922 patent claims. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages. This case provides important guidance on the § 101 eligibility boundary for digital communications technology patents.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies benefit from the affirmance of eligibility for certain communications patents and the denial of JMOL on damages, supporting enforcement of patents covering standards-essential technology.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face continued uncertainty regarding § 101 eligibility for communications technology patents, as the court found some claims require further analysis on eligibility.

impacts.caseName: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court had sufficient evidence to estop Valve under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2) from raising invalidity grounds in litigation that were not included in an earlier inter partes review petition, and whether the court adequately accounted for hindsight bias.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's application of IPR estoppel under § 315(e)(2), finding insufficient evidence for one ground and failure to account for hindsight bias for the other. The court clarified that estoppel analysis must rigorously evaluate whether a skilled searcher reasonably could have found the prior art, without the benefit of hindsight. This decision narrows the scope of IPR estoppel in patent litigation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent challengers benefit from a narrower application of IPR estoppel, preserving the ability to raise invalidity defenses in district court that were not included in prior IPR petitions.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face reduced ability to use IPR estoppel to foreclose invalidity challenges in litigation, potentially increasing defense costs and litigation uncertainty.

impacts.caseName: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a change from 'C2-C12-alkyl' to 'C1-C12-alkyl' in a patent specification constituted correction of an obvious typographical error or introduced new matter that broke the chain of priority to an earlier provisional application.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating Enanta's '953 patent as anticipated by Pfizer's public disclosure of nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid). The court held that changing 'C2' to 'C1' in a chemical substituent range was not an obvious typographical error, so the patent could not claim priority to the earlier provisional application. This ruling has significant implications for pharmaceutical patent drafting and priority claims involving chemical compound definitions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Generic drug manufacturers and competitors benefit from strict enforcement of priority requirements, preventing patent holders from retroactively expanding claim scope through alleged typographical corrections.
impacts.negativeImplications: Pharmaceutical patent holders face heightened risk from minor specification errors that can break priority chains, potentially exposing patents to intervening prior art and invalidation.

impacts.caseName: AGI SureTrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming relay devices for automated farming data collection are directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court erred in declining to find the case exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that AGI's farming data collection patents are patent-ineligible under § 101 but vacated the district court's refusal to find the case exceptional and remanded for reconsideration of attorney fees. The court found the claims directed to the abstract idea of collecting, processing, and sharing farming data using generic computer components. This decision is significant for the agricultural technology sector and patent eligibility in IoT/data collection technologies.
impacts.positiveImplications: Ag-tech companies facing patent assertions benefit from the affirmance of ineligibility for broad data-collection patents, and the remand on exceptional case status may deter meritless patent suits.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in agricultural technology and IoT data collection face continued § 101 eligibility challenges, limiting patent protection for innovations involving data capture and processing using known hardware.

impacts.caseName: mCom IP, LLC v. City National Bank of Florida
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether surviving patent claims not challenged in an IPR can be dismissed as obvious on the same grounds applied to cancelled claims, and whether attorney fees and sanctions were properly awarded under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed dismissal of a patent infringement complaint, finding surviving claims of an electronic banking patent invalid as obvious on the same grounds used in the IPR to cancel other claims. However, the court reversed the exceptional case fee award and attorney sanctions, finding insufficient grounds to support either. This case clarifies the interplay between IPR outcomes and district court invalidity determinations for surviving claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the ability to use IPR invalidity rationales to defeat surviving claims in district court, while the reversal of sanctions protects patent holders' right to litigate without undue penalty.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders whose patents survive IPR only in part face risk that surviving claims may still be invalidated in district court on the same grounds applied to cancelled claims.

impacts.caseName: A.L.M. Holding Company v. Zydex Industries Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent owner who grants an exclusive license but retains the right to sue for infringement retains sufficient exclusionary rights to establish constitutional standing to bring a patent infringement suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that a patent owner who retains the right to sue third parties for infringement has sufficient exclusionary rights to satisfy Article III standing, even after granting an exclusive license for manufacturing and commercialization. This decision provides important clarity on standing requirements for patent owners who structure licensing agreements with shared enforcement rights.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners structuring exclusive licenses benefit from confirmation that retaining litigation rights preserves standing, enabling flexible licensing arrangements without sacrificing enforcement ability.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential standing defense when patent owners retain litigation rights in licensing agreements, even where the licensee holds most commercialization rights.

impacts.caseName: KG Dongbu Steel Co., Ltd. v. United States
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Court of International Trade erred in sustaining Commerce's determination that debt-to-equity conversions conferred no countervailable benefit, and whether Commerce's original equityworthiness determinations should be reinstated.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade and directed reinstatement of Commerce's original determinations that debt-to-equity conversions by the Korean government for Dongbu Steel conferred countervailable subsidies. The court found that Commerce's original methodology for determining equityworthiness was correct and should not have been overridden on remand. This decision strengthens U.S. countervailing duty enforcement against foreign government equity subsidies in the steel industry.
impacts.positiveImplications: U.S. domestic steel producers benefit from stronger countervailing duty enforcement against foreign government subsidies, leveling the competitive playing field for steel imports.
impacts.negativeImplications: Foreign steel exporters and their U.S. importers face reinstated countervailing duties, increasing costs and potentially restricting market access for subsidized foreign steel products.

impacts.caseName: Otsuka America Pharmaceutical, Inc. v. Hetero Labs Limited
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the claim terms 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' in a weight-to-weight ratio limitation, and whether the court permissibly waived the Rule 65(c) bond requirement for a preliminary injunction pending appeal.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the preliminary injunction preventing Hetero from launching a generic version of Nuedexta but vacated the district court's waiver of the Rule 65(c) bond requirement pending appeal. The court upheld the claim construction interpreting 'dextromethorphan' and 'quinidine' to encompass salt forms. This ruling protects branded pharmaceutical revenues while clarifying that bond requirements cannot be waived even when equities favor the patent holder.
impacts.positiveImplications: Branded pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance of the preliminary injunction blocking generic entry, protecting market exclusivity during the patent term.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers face continued market exclusion, and preliminary injunction movants must post bonds even when equities strongly favor them, increasing the cost of seeking injunctive relief.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a third party that was not sued for patent infringement but filed IPR petitions challenging patents asserted against another entity can circumvent the one-year time bar of 35 U.S.C. § 315(b), and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination invalidating FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. The case raised significant questions about potential circumvention of the IPR one-year time bar by third-party petitioners filing at the deadline of the party actually sued. The court's decision to vacate on obviousness grounds leaves open the time-bar question but signals scrutiny of such arrangements.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from the vacatur of the Board's obviousness finding, preserving patent rights, and the court's apparent skepticism of third-party IPR filings designed to circumvent time-bar requirements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies relying on third-party IPR petitions as a defensive strategy face uncertainty about the validity of such petitions and potential scrutiny of coordinated filing arrangements.
